segments.narration: A physicist watched one funnel for fifty-two years and saw nothing. John Mainstone took charge of the pitch drop experiment in 1961.
Thomas Parnell poured hot pitch into a sealed funnel at the University of Queensland in 1927. He cut the stem three years later.
Then it just hung there. Pitch looks like a solid you could shatter, but it flows, over a hundred billion times thicker than water.
Nine drops have fallen in ninety-nine years. Mainstone missed the 1988 one by stepping out for a drink, and a webcam failed in 2000.
He died in 2013, months before the ninth drop broke free. Nobody has ever seen one fall in person.

research.summary: Thomas Parnell poured heated pitch into a sealed glass funnel at the University of Queensland in 1927 to show that a substance that looks solid is a very viscous fluid. The stem was cut in October 1930; the first drop fell in December 1938 and nine have fallen in total, the ninth separating on 24 April 2014. John Mainstone, custodian from 1961, missed the seventh drop in 1988 because he had stepped out for a drink, and a webcam glitch lost the eighth in 2000; he died on 13 August 2013 without ever seeing one fall. Wikipedia puts the pitch at about 230 billion times the viscosity of water while the University of Queensland's own page says 100 billion, so the narration uses the conservative 'over a hundred billion'. Mainstone and Parnell were given the 2005 Ig Nobel Prize in physics for the experiment.

factual_claims.text: The Lycurgus Cup appears jade green in reflected light and blood red when light is transmitted through it.
The Lycurgus Cup is a Roman cage cup made in the fourth century AD, perhaps around 290 to 325 AD, and cut from glass.
The Lycurgus Cup is the only complete Roman glass object made from this dichroic glass.
In 1990 researchers examining fragments under a microscope found gold and silver particles about seventy nanometres across dispersed in the glass.
The colour shift is caused by the way those metal particles scatter and absorb light, and the makers probably did not understand or control the process.

segments.narration: Light from behind turns this Roman cup blood red. In daylight the same glass is jade green. One object, two colours.
It was carved in the fourth century, probably around 290 to 325 AD, from a single block of glass, then cut away.
So how does one cup hold two colours? Nobody could explain it for centuries, and it is the only complete Roman piece like it.
In 1990 researchers put fragments under a microscope. The glass is salted with gold and silver particles about seventy nanometres across.
Those specks scatter and absorb light differently depending on where it comes from. Roman glassmakers likely stumbled onto it by accident, and never fully controlled it.

research.summary: The Lycurgus Cup is a fourth-century Roman cage cup, possibly made in Alexandria or Rome around 290 to 325 AD, and the only complete Roman object made of this dichroic glass. It reads jade green in reflected light and blood red in transmitted light. The glass carries gold and silver dispersed as colloids, roughly 330 parts per million silver and 40 parts per million gold, in particles about 70 nanometres across, visible only by transmission electron microscopy; the colour flip comes from a surface plasmon resonance effect, the fine particles scattering blue more than red in transmitted light. Smithsonian reports that researchers in England identified the particles in broken fragments in 1990 and gives the particle size as about 50 nanometres, against Wikipedia's 70, so the narration uses Wikipedia's figure and the sources disagree on the exact size. The two sources also differ on intent: Wikipedia says the process remains unclear and was probably neither well understood nor controlled, likely found through accidental contamination with ground gold and silver, while Smithsonian suggests the precise mixture points to deliberate skill. The narration follows the more cautious reading. The cup is in the British Museum, bought from Lord Rothschild in 1958 for 20,000 pounds, and shows King Lycurgus entangled in a vine with Ambrosia, Dionysus, a satyr, Pan and a panther.

segments.narration: Eighty sheep were shipped to a Scottish island in 1942. Gruinard, in Gruinard Bay, a kilometre off the Wester Ross coast.
Porton Down scientists detonated anthrax bombs beside tethered groups of them. The sheep began dying within days. The bombs were part of Operation Vegetarian.
The plan was never used on anyone, and the cakes were destroyed. So why did the island stay shut for nearly half a century?
Anthrax spores survive in soil for decades. Warning signs went up, visits were banned, and only inspectors landed to test the ground.
In 1986 crews soaked the island in 280 tonnes of formaldehyde. A test flock stayed healthy, and the signs came down in April 1990.

research.summary: Gruinard Island is a 196-hectare island in Gruinard Bay, Highland, about a kilometre offshore between Gairloch and Ullapool. In 1942 scientists from the biology department at Porton Down took eighty sheep there and detonated anthrax bombs near tethered groups of them, using the Vollum 14578 strain; the sheep began dying within days. The work supported Operation Vegetarian, an unused plan to drop anthrax-laced linseed cakes on German cattle; the cakes were destroyed without being used. The island was requisitioned in 1942 and quarantined indefinitely, with visits banned except for Porton Down contamination checks. Decontamination began in 1986, spraying about 280 tonnes of formaldehyde solution diluted in seawater over the island and removing the most contaminated topsoil; a flock placed in 1987 stayed healthy. On 24 April 1990, after 48 years of quarantine, junior defence minister Michael Neubert removed the warning signs, and on 1 May 1990 the original owner's heirs repurchased the island for 500 pounds. Sky History corroborates the 1942 programme, the linseed-cake plan and its destruction, the sheep dying within days, the formaldehyde spraying and the 1990 announcement, but gives no sheep count and does not date the spraying.

The Mount Owen moa foot retains muscle and sinew attached to the bone.

segments.narration: A bird's foot sat in a cave for 3,300 years. Cavers found it on Mount Owen, near Nelson, in January 1987.
It was not a fossil. Muscle and sinew were still attached to the bone, dried hard and unmistakably there.
The foot belonged to an upland moa, a flightless bird under a metre tall. So why did the cave keep it and not the rest?
Dry, cold cave air stops decay almost completely. Outside, every other upland moa was gone within a century of people reaching New Zealand.
So the foot is older than the extinction that erased its species. It now sits in Te Papa, in Wellington, catalogued as specimen S.023808.

research.summary: Wikipedia's moa article records a complete foot of Megalapteryx didinus, the upland moa, found in a cave on Mount Owen near Nelson, New Zealand, in the 1980s, held by Te Papa Tongarewa. The Megalapteryx article dates the find precisely: a foot with some muscle and sinews, found on 7 January 1987 at Mount Owen, about 3,300 to 3,400 years old, catalogued NMNZ S.023808. The upland moa stood under a metre tall and weighed about 17 to 34 kilograms, among the smallest moa. The two articles are not fully consistent on extinction: the moa article says moa died out within 100 years of human settlement, primarily from overhunting, with all moa extinct by 1445 CE, while the Megalapteryx lead says that species went extinct around 1500 CE. The narration avoids a single extinction date and says 'within a century of people reaching New Zealand', which both support. The cave provenance comes from the moa article; the Megalapteryx entry names only Mount Owen and does not repeat the cave detail, and neither article mentions surviving skin or claws, so the narration claims only muscle and sinew.

factual_claims.text: Sigiriya in central Sri Lanka is a column of granite about 180 metres high carrying a fifth-century royal complex.
The Lion Gate partway up Sigiriya is flanked by sculpted lion's paws, and the lion's head that once sat above them has collapsed.
Paintings would have covered an area of the western rock face about 140 metres long, and a 2010 report counted 22 surviving frescoes.
The Culavamsa says Kashyapa moved his capital to the secure summit of Sigiriya to guard against the return of his half-brother Moggallana.

segments.narration: A palace sat on top of a 180-metre rock. Sigiriya, in central Sri Lanka, built in the fifth century.
Halfway up, the stairs pass between two giant carved lion's paws. The head that once sat above them collapsed long ago.
Paintings once covered 140 metres of the western cliff, and twenty-two of them survive. Who goes to this much trouble to live on a rock?
The chronicles give a reason. Kashyapa had seized the throne, and he feared his half-brother Moggallana would come back to take it.
Moggallana came back in 495 and won. The capital moved away, monks took over the rock, and later visitors scratched 685 poems into its polished wall.

research.summary: Sigiriya is a massive column of granite about 180 metres high in central Sri Lanka, with a summit elevation of 349 metres. The Culavamsa credits King Kashyapa, given as CE 477 to 495 in the text and 473 to 491 in the article's royal template, with developing it into a city and fortress, and says he moved the capital to the secure summit to guard against the return of his half-brother Moggallana; Moggallana defeated him in 495 CE and moved the capital back to Anuradhapura, after which the site became a Buddhist monastery complex. Alternatives are recorded, including Dhatusena as primary builder and a reading in which the site had no military function. The Lion Gate sits on a plateau partway up, flanked by sculpted lion's paws, with a head above them that collapsed. Paintings would have covered an area of the western face 140 metres long and 40 metres high; a 2010 report refers to 22 frescoes, fading since 1930. The mirror wall is plastered brick, once polished enough to reflect the king, and Paranavithana deciphered 685 verses written on it between the 8th and 10th centuries, though the same article elsewhere refers to more than 1,500 poems and does not reconcile the two counts; the narration uses the lower, attributed figure. Sigiriya was inscribed by UNESCO in 1982 as the Ancient City of Sigiriya, reference 202. The UNESCO listing page and two secondary corroborating pages returned HTTP 403 from this environment, so every claim here rests on the Wikipedia article alone and the two internally inconsistent figures are flagged rather than resolved.

verification.note: Wikipedia describes a massive column of granite approximately 180 m high and credits fifth-century development to Kashyapa. The infobox gives a 349 m elevation, which is height above sea level rather than above the plain, so the narration uses 180 metres.

verification.claim: The Lion Gate partway up Sigiriya is flanked by sculpted lion's paws, and the lion's head that once sat above them has collapsed.

factual_claims.text: At Kaali on Saaremaa, Estonia, a stone wall was built around the main meteorite crater lake in the early Iron Age.
The main Kaali crater is 110 metres in diameter and 22 metres deep and holds a lake, with eight smaller craters 12 to 40 metres across lying within one kilometre.
The Kaali meteoroid struck at an estimated 10 to 20 kilometres per second, broke up at 5 to 10 kilometres altitude, and released about 80 terajoules, roughly 20 kilotons of TNT.
The area was populated at the time of impact, but published estimates of when it happened range from about 7,600 to about 3,000 years ago.
The early Iron Age wall around the Kaali lake was about 470 metres long and the bones of horses, sheep, oxen and other domestic animals were found inside it, and the lake was regarded as sacred.

segments.narration: Iron Age islanders built a wall around a meteorite crater. Kaali, on Saaremaa, off the coast of Estonia.
The main crater is 110 metres wide and 22 metres deep, now filled with water. Eight smaller ones lie within a kilometre.
The rock came in at up to 20 kilometres a second and broke apart in the air. The blast was close to a small nuclear bomb.
And people were living there when it hit, though nobody agrees when that was, with estimates running from about 7,600 to 3,000 years ago. So what do you build after the sky explodes?
A 470-metre stone wall around the lake, with animal bones heaped inside, horses, sheep, oxen. Estonians called it the holy lake.

research.summary: Kaali is a field of nine meteorite craters at Kaali village on Saaremaa, Estonia. The main crater is 110 m across and 22 m deep and holds a lake; eight smaller craters, 12 to 40 m across and 1 to 4 m deep, lie within a kilometre. The meteoroid is estimated at 20 to 80 tonnes travelling 10 to 20 km/s, breaking up at 5 to 10 km altitude; the main fragment excavated about 81,000 cubic metres of dolomite and released roughly 80 TJ, about 20 kilotons of TNT, comparable to the Hiroshima bomb, incinerating vegetation within about 6 km. segments.narration: Eleven churches in Ethiopia were carved downward out of bedrock. Lalibela, up in the Amhara highlands. No blocks, no mortar, no scaffolding.
Crews cut trenches straight down into volcanic rock, then hollowed out the block they had left standing in the middle. Roof first. Floor last.
Four of them stand completely free of the mountain. Tunnels run between the groups. One, Bete Giyorgis, is a giant cross sunk into the ground.
Tradition gives all of it to one king, Gebre Meskel Lalibela, around 1200, and says the eleven took twenty-four years. The rock disagrees.
Archaeologist David Phillipson dated the earliest cuttings to the seventh or eighth century. Four or five building phases, five hundred years of work, and one king's name on the whole thing.

research.summary: Lalibela, in Amhara, Ethiopia, holds eleven medieval rock-hewn churches: four free-standing monoliths and seven still attached to the mountain, carved downward from living scoriaceous basalt with hammers and chisels, with trenches around them and tunnels linking two of the groups. Biete Giorgis is cruciform and free-standing. Tradition credits the Zagwe king Gebre Meskel Lalibela (reign c. 1181-1221) and holds the eleven took 24 years, with the town conceived as a second Jerusalem. Cambridge archaeologist David Phillipson argues the oldest rock-hewn features may date to the 7th or 8th centuries, about 500 years earlier than the traditional dating, with the last phase under the king whose name the town bears; the Metropolitan Museum states scholars generally agree on four or five phases between the 7th and 13th centuries. UNESCO inscribed the site in 1978. The local legend recorded by the sources checked involves Christ and Jerusalem, not angels, so no angel legend appears in the script.
